data.title: LMT Gets $740M Awards, GD, RTX Pick Up Missile Contracts – A Look At This Week’s Defense Deals
data.description:
Key points:
  • Lockheed Martin secured around $740 million in defense awards related to F-35 fighter jets and C-5 transport aircraft.
  • General Dynamics and RTX picked up additional military contracts for Stryker armored vehicles and rolling airframe missiles
  • Elbit Systems reported a 17% increase in Q3 revenue to $2.25 billion, while order backlog reached $33 billion.

Defense contractors were in focus this week as Lockheed Martin (LMT), General Dynamics (GD) and RTX (RTX) secured new multi-million-dollar contracts, while Elbit Systems (ESLT) reported topline growth in the third quarter.

The U.S. Navy also selected 28 companies for an electronic-warfare program with a combined contract ceiling exceeding $7.1 billion.

Lockheed Martin Picks Up $740M In Defense Awards

Lockheed Martin received a $330.6 million Navy contract modification on Thursday for materials and components needed to produce 75 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets for the U.S. military. A day earlier, the company secured a $316.6 million Air Force contract for logistics and maintenance support for C-5 Galaxy transport aircraft.

That followed a $93.2 million Navy order on Tuesday for F-35 maintenance and sustainment, including cybersecurity upgrades and specialized repair capabilities.

The three deals carried a combined value of roughly $740 million.

General Dynamics, RTX Add To Contract Wins

General Dynamics secured a $332.5 million Army contract on Wednesday for maintenance, training and other support services for its Stryker armored vehicles. Its Mission Systems unit also received a $20.5 million Navy modification deal on Tuesday for submarine combat-system software.

Meanwhile, RTX’s Raytheon unit received a $120.3 million Navy modification award on Thursday to produce Rolling Airframe Missiles for the U.S. Navy. That followed a separate $12.3 million modification contract for engineering and technical support on the missile system.

Separately, Elbit Systems reported third-quarter (Q3) revenue of $2.25 billion Tuesday, up 17% year over year but marginally below Street estimates, according to Fiscal.ai. Earnings per share rose to $4.36 from $3.35, while its order backlog climbed to $33 billion.

Navy Names 28 Contractors For $7.1B Program

On Thursday, the Navy announced a $7.13 billion multiple-award contract under its Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program, which helps warships detect and counter enemy threats.

Recipients include Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics, RTX, Northrop Grumman (NOC), Leidos (LDOS), CACI International (CACI), HII (HII), Amentum (AMTM) and Frequency Electronics (FEIM).

Despite the contract wins, shares of Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics, RTX and Elbit Systems fell 5.1%, 4.24%, 2.45% and 1.45%, respectively, this week.

data.title: From ChatGPT to Claude deals: Walmart looks like an agentic AI winner
data.description:
Walmart developed its generative AI shopping assistant Sparky to very little fanfare as part of a broader push into what it called adaptive retail. While early buzz was light, the payoff for Walmart investing in Sparky is just beginning.

CEO John Furner noted that in Walmart's third quarter, U.S. usage of Sparky climbed 129% year over year, with baskets associated with the assistant running 40% larger. The AI assistant helps shoppers discover items, plan meals, summarize reviews, turn photos of handwritten lists into carts, and reorder staples based on inventory positioning, pricing, and delivery speed.

Walmart began its efforts to scale generative AI across customers, members, associates, and partners in 2024. The retail giant introduced Sparky in June 2025 inside its app and web experience, pairing text chat with voice and image inputs. Rather than relying on a single bot for everything, Walmart structured its AI ecosystem around specialized agents, separating shopping discovery in Sparky from dedicated customer-support automation that handles order lookup, returns, and delivery updates. The company also expanded beyond proprietary surfaces by partnering earlier this year with OpenAI to bring Sparky into ChatGPT and building a Google Gemini shopping experience.

Meanwhile, Anthropic partnered with Walmart to help power Sparky itself using Claude models such as Claude Sonnet 4.6. On the consumer side, rather than embedding a standalone Sparky widget inside Claude, Walmart opened its Agent Gateway, built on Anthropic's Model Context Protocol, in October. This allows approved third-party assistants, including Claude, to search Walmart's catalog and prepare orders directly on a shopper's behalf using user-controlled Agent Profiles and spending limits.

Looking ahead, Walmart plans to scale Sparky across more markets, languages, and shopping modes while building infrastructure for third-party AI agents. It has already rolled Sparky out in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, and Sam's Club with support for languages such as Spanish and French. Next, Walmart is introducing Agent Profiles so shoppers can set permissions, spending limits, track agent purchases separately, or revoke access, alongside a Walmart Agent Gateway to govern how approved external agents interact with its catalog.

Emma Tucker

1. FROM MY DESK

What was supposed to be a triumphant week for (Anthropic) has devolved into a Wall Street blame game.

The company's highly anticipated debut was meant to reassure investors about AI's future. Instead, its shares fell 8.5% on its second day of trading Friday, wiping $109 billion from its market value. Now investors are questioning everything from who got shares to whether the opening price was set too high. The trouble goes well beyond Anthropic: Nasdaq stocks lost more than $4 trillion in value this week, erasing the index's gains for the year.

Behind Anthropic's debut are siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who have built a company that prides itself on being anything but ordinary. Our reporters take you inside the brother-sister partnership at the top of what's still one of the world's most valuable companies.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

2. TODAY'S HEADLINES

  • The White House plans to scale back its use of "special government employees," who can work for the government while retaining their private-sector salaries or investments.
  • New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have forged an unlikely partnership that has helped keep crime low and reassured business and Jewish community leaders. Making it work has required compromises.
  • A California jury found a man guilty of intentionally sparking the 2025 fire that devastated Los Angeles's Pacific Palisades.
  • Citadel Chief Executive Ken Griffin spent at least five years courting elite universities to bring a top technology school to Miami, hoping to turn his new home into a global business hub. He ultimately struck a $3 billion deal with Carnegie Mellon University.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

France's riots are testing its colorblind ideals.

Student protests over school conditions spiraled into riots, setting off a fierce debate over who was responsible. A far-right leader pointed to neighborhoods with large immigrant populations, a prominent far-left politician blamed police tactics, and the government cited ultraleft agitators. But France's longstanding commitment to colorblindness bars the state from collecting statistics on race and ethnicity, complicating efforts to understand the unrest. Stacy Meichtry and Bertrand Benoit write about the political taboo tearing France apart.

5.

Welcome to the age of everything breaking.

(Microsoft) Outlook went dark. Air-traffic control grounded every departing U.S. flight. Then came outages at banks, airlines and even the National Security Agency. The failures appear to have different technical causes, but they underscore the vulnerabilities of our hyperconnected world, where aging systems and the race to fix security flaws pose growing challenges. In a darkly funny Saturday essay, Joel Stein explores why the bigger concern may not be the outages themselves, but our ability to recover from them-and how to get by when technology lets us down.

The economics of growing old. From rising elder-care costs to the pressures of caring for children and aging parents, our new series explores how America's aging population is reshaping household finances and everyday life. The number of countries Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has visited across five continents since taking office in March 2025. He has spent 113 days, or nearly 20% of his time in office, traveling abroad-more than twice as much time as President Trump over the same period. The globe-trotting is part of Carney's push to forge new trade and security partnerships and reduce Canada's reliance on the U.S. as Trump's tariffs and annexation threats strain relations between the neighbors.

He writes in his underwear. Now millions of men are reading his books.

Matt Dinniman used to sell cat-themed art on (Etsy). Now he is the unlikely literary sensation behind "Dungeon Crawler Carl," a wildly popular fantasy series about a man in boxer shorts and a talking cat competing in a deadly alien game show. What began as a self-published series has sold more than 20 million copies and inspired men to read fiction en masse. Dinniman, who wrote the books in his underpants while eating Twizzlers, has become so famous that he is moving to a gated community, partly because fans keep knocking on his door.

data.title: How a brutal week for stocks almost wiped out their gains for the entire year
data.description:
By Joy Wiltermuth and Claudia Assis

Investors are now more focused on protecting their portfolios than looking for bargains

Fear on Wall Street is running high as the Nasdaq swings to a yearly loss and the Dow and S&P 500 give back most of their 2026 gains.

There wasn't much left of the stock market's earlier robust gains for 2026 after Friday's carnage.

Investors dumped artificial-intelligence beneficiaries Nvidia (NVDA), Sandisk (SNDK) and Micron (MU), alongside defensive stocks like Costco (COST), leaving few areas of the market unscathed ahead of the holiday-shortened Thanksgiving week.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA closed below the 50,000 threshold for a second straight day, joining the S&P 500 index SPX and Nasdaq Composite COMP in at least a 10% correction from their previous record closes.

Under the surface, things looked even more dire. A tally on Friday showed that 64% of the S&P 500's constituents closed at least 20% below their record highs, according to Dow Jones Market Data. That figure reached as high as 87% for the battered information-technology sector.

The S&P 500's information-technology sector has all but a sliver of its constituents down 20% or more from their record highs

"We are in the midst of a re-evaluation and a correction," said Jim Caron, chief investment officer of portfolio solutions at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Earnings and the economy still look good for next year, Caron said. But anxiety has only grown around the artificial-intelligence trade, especially with new scrutiny in Washington into sales of Nvidia's chips to China. There's also the U.S. midterm elections, which exposed how deeply unpopular the data-center boom has been with voters.

"It's not just about circular financing," Caron said, nor concerns about the speed of returns on AI investments. It's also a bigger conversation about how to build data centers in communities in a more sustainable and durable way. "We can't have a data center go in and everyone's electricity bill goes up," he added.

The hope was that Nvidia's stellar earnings and Anthropic's (ANT) historic IPO would staunch the bleeding this week in markets. And there was hope that investors might take heart in the economy's resilience and start picking through the stock-market carnage for bargains.

Instead, as of Friday the S&P 500 was up only 1% for the year, while the Dow was 0.2% higher and the Nasdaq was down 2.7%, according to FactSet.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 NDX was down 0.9% for the year, off more than 19% from its record high and on the cusp of a bear market.

Into the void

"It's a buyers' strike, even though we now have lower valuations," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services. There's also little clarity on what the next catalysts could be to shift sentiment back to a more positive direction, he said.

Stocks staged a dramatic rebound after President Donald Trump's April 9, 2025, pause on most of his reciprocal tariffs, as feverish dip-buying quickly erased the fallout in financial markets. The same pattern repeated several times during the first part of Trump's second term in the White House.

But with the "blue wave" soon putting control of the House and Senate in the hands of Democrats, Wall Street no longer expects an executive order or a social-media post that can shift market sentiment in an instant.

Is the AI punchbowl gone?

Investors have begun treating the midterm results as the moment the punchbowl was removed from the AI party.

"The midterms got rid of the assumption that there won't be pushback against data centers," said Keith Buchanan, a fund manager at Globalt Investments. "It made that part of it real."

As part of this, valuations in the stock market have come down dramatically. The S&P 500's information-technology sector was trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 16.3, based on Thursday's close, which was the lowest since the March 2020 COVID crisis, according to John Butters, a senior earnings analyst at FactSet. That's down from a 22 ratio at the beginning of 2026.

"This is almost like an epic rethink of the sector," said Truist's Lerner. "What it tells me is that people have lost confidence in the earnings outlook."

Wall Street now expects peak earnings growth this year, but for the S&P 500 to still see 16% to 17% earnings growth next year. But comments from Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller suggest the 2027 backdrop could be less business-friendly. He's been at the forefront in warning that a "shock" may be needed to coax inflation back down to the central bank's 2% annual target.

The Fed's next decision on rates is Dec. 9, with the odds favoring back-to-back rate hikes through January, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

Investors worry the Fed could tighten financial conditions too much and damage the economy.

The gloom hasn't improved even though global oil prices (BRN00) have tumbled almost 20% so far in November. Instead, Wall Street's "fear gauge" has surged more than 50% over the same stretch, with the below chart showing the Cboe Volatility Index VIX jump's above 30 on Friday.

When the "VIX" spikes, it implies there will be increased volatility in the S&P 500 over the next 30 days. That backdrop suggests investors might be more focused on protecting their portfolios, rather than looking to buy cheaper stocks.

As Caron at Morgan Stanley put it, "What's left over is the emotional aspect of preserving gains for the year."

Mike DeStefano contributed

-Joy Wiltermuth -Claudia Assis

This content was created by MarketWatch, which is operated by Dow Jones & Co. MarketWatch is published independently from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: India’s Forex Reserves Fall $14.21 Bn To $705.34 Bn
data.description:
Decline in foreign currency assets and gold holdings accounts for most of the weekly fall, RBI data shows

India’s foreign exchange reserves declined by USD 14.21 billion to USD 705.34 billion in the week ended 13 November, according to the latest data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Total reserves stood at USD 719.55 billion in the previous week ended 6 November.

The decline was led by a fall in foreign currency assets (FCAs) and gold reserves, which together accounted for most of the weekly reduction.

FCAs, the largest component of the reserves, fell by USD 7.90 billion to USD 583.45 billion during the reported week. Expressed in dollar terms, FCAs include the impact of appreciation or depreciation in non-US currencies such as the euro, pound and yen held in the reserves.

“There was dollar sale of USD 1.57 billion and rest is revaluation loss led by gold,” said Gaura Sen Gupta, Chief Economist at IDFC First Bank.

Gold reserves declined by USD 6.18 billion to USD 98.61 billion during the week. Special drawing rights (SDRs) fell by USD 92 million to USD 18.52 billion, while India’s reserve position with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) decreased by USD 32 million to USD 4.76 billion, the RBI data showed.

India’s foreign exchange reserves are now around USD 80.4 billion below their all-time high of USD 785.7 billion, recorded in the week ended 4 September.

The record level followed significant foreign currency inflows through a special concessional swap scheme for diaspora deposits.

In the previous week ended 6 November, reserves had increased, primarily due to a USD 2.205 billion rise in gold holdings.

Rupee Under Pressure From Rising US Treasury Yields

The rupee remained under pressure during the reported week amid rising yields on US Treasury securities.

On 12 November, the Indian currency closed 0.37 per cent lower at 94.04 against the US dollar. Dealers cited dollar purchases by state-run banks ahead of the release of Consumer Price Index data.

The rupee has depreciated by 3.02 per cent so far in calendar year 2026, while it has appreciated by 2.31 per cent in financial year 2026-27 so far.

The weekly movement in reserves reflects changes in foreign currency holdings and the valuation of assets, including gold and non-US currencies.

data.title: Solana ETFs Defy Wall Street’s Big Crypto Sell-Off
data.description:
Solana was the only major US spot crypto ETF category to attract new money last week, while Bitcoin and Ethereum funds continued losing billions. However, almost all of Solana’s inflows came from a single day.

According to SoSoValue, Solana ETFs recorded $4.4 million in weekly inflows, ending six consecutive weeks of withdrawals.

Almost all the buying happened on Monday, November 16, when investors poured $11.7 million into Solana funds. Bitwise’s Solana Staking ETF (BSOL) received roughly $10.8 million.

The remaining four trading days brought withdrawals or no inflows.

Interestingly, Bitwise published its bullish Solana forecast that same Monday, predicting SOL could reach $1,100 by 2031 if tokenized stock trading expands significantly.

Whether that forecast influenced investors remains unclear.

Why Solana Stood Alone as Crypto ETFs Lost Billions

The broader market saw heavy selling.

Bitcoin ETFs lost more than $1 billion for a third consecutive week. BlackRock’s IBIT alone suffered a record $541 million withdrawal on Thursday.

Ethereum ETFs extended their weekly outflow streak to eight weeks. XRP, Hyperliquid and Zcash funds also recorded withdrawals.

What’s Next for Solana Price?

Despite attracting ETF inflows, Solana’s price continued falling. SOL dropped to $65.82 on Friday, losing approximately 13% over seven days.

The altcoin’s next support is near $62. Recovering above $68 could offer some relief.

Meanwhile, Solana ETFs held approximately $965 million in assets on November 20, compared with $1.41 billion in cumulative net inflows since launch.

Although that gap does not directly measure investors’ losses, it reflects the sharp decline in fund asset values.

For now, Solana’s ETF recovery remains fragile. Next week’s flows will reveal whether institutional demand is returning or Monday’s buying was an exception.

data.title: Goldman Sachs Market Panic Index Hit 9 out of 10 – What Does It Mean?
data.description:
US stocks suffered another brutal session on Friday, November 20, as Goldman Sachs warned that the selloff “has legs.” The bank’s Panic Index climbed to 9 out of 10.

Bitcoin has not escaped the pressure, and the coming week could prove decisive for both markets.

The Stock Market Selloff Could Continue Further

Commodity trading advisers, or CTAs, are systematic funds that buy and sell based on price trends. When markets fall, their models often force them to sell more.

According to Goldman’s trading desk, as Bloomberg reported, CTAs have already sold $57 billion in equities over the past month.

As a result, their net position in US stocks has flipped to a $19 billion short.

Goldman’s models suggest more selling ahead. These funds could unload another $65.8 billion in a flat market, or $28.6 billion if stocks rebound. If the decline deepens, sales could reach $80.6 billion.

The damage is already severe.

  • The Nasdaq 100 posted its worst week since March 2020, dropping 5.6% on Friday alone.
  • Meanwhile, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 11%.
  • NVIDIA has now fallen nearly 50% from its early October peak.

In total, Friday’s rout erased about $2.5 trillion from US stocks, bringing 45-day losses to roughly $8.9 trillion.

Investors have grown reluctant to buy the dip amid doubts about returns on massive AI spending. Even Anthropic’s IPO failed to revive risk appetite.

How Is Bitcoin Holding Up in the Selloff?

So far, Bitcoin has offered little shelter. The cryptocurrency fell near $55,000, which extended its monthly decline to around 30%. It now sits roughly 55% below its $126,080 all-time high from October 2025.

Moreover, spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded roughly $3.47 billion in outflows this month alone. That steady exodus has removed an important source of demand.

Analysts at Wintermute and other firms see potential downside toward the $50,000-$54,000 zone.

That range aligns with Bitcoin’s realized price and historical support levels.

The realized price reflects the average price at which all coins last moved on-chain. A drop to $50,000 would mean a further decline of about 12%.

Some traders view current levels as approaching a cycle bottom. However, others warn of deeper losses if equities stay weak and the Federal Reserve remains hawkish.

Why Does Bitcoin Keep Falling With Stocks?

The answer lies in correlation. Since 2020, Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq has climbed from near zero to around 0.4. That link has tightened as institutions increasingly hold Bitcoin alongside tech stocks.

In fact, Bitcoin has declined on roughly three-quarters of the Nasdaq’s significant down days, often by an average of 2%.

Grayscale and DWF Labs have also noted that Bitcoin still trades like a high-beta risk asset during market stress.

Meanwhile, its longer-term volatility has moderated, according to those same analyses. Still, not everyone sees only downside.

Michaël van de Poppe points to signs of capitulation, including rising volume and broken support levels.

In his view, these conditions could create accumulation opportunities.

For now, Goldman’s warning suggests that risk assets could face more headwinds. Investors will watch equity flows, ETF activity, and upcoming economic data for signs of exhaustion.

data.title: Bitcoin clears its largest liquidation cluster between $59K and $62K
data.description:
Bitcoin just walked through the minefield. The largest liquidation cluster on Glassnode's six-month futures heatmap, sitting between $59K and $62K, was fully cleared on November 20, 2026.

That matters because the cluster was a stockpile of forced selling waiting below the market price. Now it's gone, and whatever comes next won't be driven by that particular pile of leveraged longs getting margin-called.

On-chain analytics firm Glassnode flagged the $59K to $62K range as the single largest such zone on its six-month futures liquidation heatmap. The positions were mostly leveraged longs, meaning traders who borrowed to bet on higher prices.

According to Glassnode, the cluster traced back to long entries opened in August 2026. Those trades piled in after a sharp price surge in mid-August, when optimism was running hot.

Glassnode reported on November 21 that the cluster had been fully cleared the day before. The move itself was not gentle. Bitcoin slid from approximately $63K to a close of around $58.3K to $59.5K on November 20, 2026, pushing straight through the zone.

November has been a rough month for anyone holding Bitcoin with borrowed money. The price had previously topped out in the $74K to $77K range before sliding to lows around $57K to $59K by November 20 and 21.

As Bitcoin drifted toward the cluster in mid-November, the zone was already being identified as a critical risk area. Estimates at the time warned that liquidations could exceed $1 billion at $62K alone. If the full cluster gave way, those same estimates put potential liquidations at up to nearly $2 billion.

The pressure wasn't coming from leverage alone. Outflows from US Bitcoin ETFs crossed $1.5 billion, a sign that traditional investors using regulated wrappers were heading for the exits too.

Meanwhile, stablecoin supply contracted by $14 billion to $17 billion over the 30 days leading up to the event.

The most direct effect is mechanical. A major source of automatic selling below the current price has been removed, which may ease some of the downward pressure that comes from cascading liquidations.

The clearance removes a known downside risk, but it doesn't fix the broader picture. Any rebound would likely depend on whether outside conditions improve, particularly ETF flows and stablecoin supply.

ETF flows have become one of the clearest windows into institutional demand, and right now that window shows people leaving the room. A $14 billion to $17 billion drop in stablecoin supply over a month means less liquidity sitting inside crypto, ready to buy dips.

For longer-term holders, the clearance of the August longs closes a chapter that began with a mid-August surge and ended with a November flush. The speculative excess from that rally has been largely wrung out of the futures market, at least in this price band.

data.title: Southern California port employers, watchmen union reach tentative deal
data.description:
The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) employers group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports said on Saturday it had reached a tentative agreement with the union for security guards, averting a strike that could have disrupted operations at the two busiest cargo shipping hubs in the US.

The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents 250 security officers, or watchmen, who account for a small fraction of the ports' workforce, but their work is critical because they control access at terminal gates, conduct security patrols and report safety issues.

PMA, which represents terminal owners, said the agreement reached on Saturday was subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the current contract will be extended pending ratification.

The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

The two sides resumed federally mediated negotiations on Friday, two days after the parties broke off talks, with the employers group reporting "little-to-no movement from the union on PMA's proposals."

The PMA said at the time that its offer included a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each union member and a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000.

The offer also called for maintaining fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, valued at more than $62,000 each year, and increased pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure.

Talks between the terminal owners and the union have stretched on for more than a year.

data.title: Goldman Sachs warns US stock selloff could worsen next week
data.description:
Goldman Sachs says the pain in US stocks may not be finished. The bank warned that the selloff could deepen next week, after its proprietary Panic Index climbed to 9 out of 10 on November 20, 2026.

Crypto-linked equities are absorbing some of the damage. Goldman's bitcoin-sensitive stock basket has dropped 11%, outpacing several of the bank's other thematic trackers.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6%, its worst weekly showing since March 2020.

Semiconductors fared even worse. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 11%, matching the drop in Goldman's bitcoin-sensitive basket.

Nvidia has slid nearly 50% from its early-October peak.

Goldman's other thematic baskets tell a similar story. Its retail-favorites index declined 8.9%, while its cyclical-versus-defensive basket slipped 3.2%.

The core of Goldman's warning centers on commodity trading advisors, or CTAs. These are systematic funds that follow price trends: when markets go up, they buy, and when markets go down, they sell.

Over the past month, CTAs sold $57 billion in US equities. That selling flipped them to a $19 billion net short position, meaning they are now positioned to profit if stocks fall further.

Goldman's models suggest these funds could unload another $28.6 billion to $80.6 billion, depending on where markets head.

Goldman also pointed to momentum traders as a primary driver of the recent decline. Both institutional and retail investors have been shedding risk assets.

Two threads run through the current downturn. The first is growing skepticism about whether the enormous sums being poured into AI infrastructure will produce returns that justify the spending.

The second thread is the lack of a fresh catalyst. The much-anticipated Anthropic IPO did not deliver the risk-on boost some investors may have hoped for.

For crypto investors, the 11% drop in Goldman's bitcoin-sensitive basket is the clearest signal. These are publicly traded companies whose fortunes tend to move with Bitcoin, and they are falling alongside the broader tech complex.

The weakness in the retail-favorites basket adds to that picture. Retail-preferred assets and crypto-related equities often share an investor base, and both are being sold as risk appetite fades.

What to watch next week comes down to a few markers. Whether the Nasdaq 100 can find a floor after its worst week since March 2020 will shape how much additional selling CTAs carry out.

Nvidia's trajectory is another key indicator. As the most prominent AI stock, its near-50% slide from the October peak has become shorthand for broader doubts about the sector.

With the Anthropic IPO failing to spark a rally, the market currently lacks an obvious reason to reverse course, and Goldman's models suggest that, absent one, systematic sellers could keep pressing.

data.title: Elon Musk Calls Anthropic’s Models ‘Great Products,’ Jassy Says ‘We’re Big Believers’: Mag 7 Voices This Week
data.description:
Key points:
  • Musk said Anthropic is “extremely likely” to keep renting computing capacity from SpaceX and could seek another 10 gigawatts.
  • Amazon CEO Andy Jassy reiterated that his company is a “big believer” in Anthropic ahead of its Nasdaq debut.
  • Amazon and Alphabet’s Google are set to own approximately 14.7% and 13.7% of Anthropic, respectively, following the IPO and private placement.

Anthropic’s landmark IPO put the AI company’s relationships with some of the biggest technology companies in focus this week.

Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet’s Google (GOOGL) and Nvidia (NVDA) are among its investors, while Microsoft (MSFT) is a major financial backer and infrastructure partner. SpaceX, led by Tesla (TSLA) CEO Elon Musk, is also supplying computing capacity to the Claude developer.

The company priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, before beginning trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, listing at $111.50.

Among the executives, Musk praised Anthropic’s AI models and said the company was likely to continue renting computing capacity from SpaceX. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy also reaffirmed his support for the AI developer.

Here’s what the leaders of the Magnificent Seven companies said about Anthropic and its IPO this week:

Musk Praises Anthropic As SpaceX Eyes More Compute Business

Musk praised two of Anthropic’s AI models ahead of the company’s Nasdaq debut. He said he had met members of the team before SpaceX agreed to supply computing capacity to Anthropic and knew several employees from his time at OpenAI.

“Opus and Fable are great products.”

Elon Musk, CEO, SpaceX and Tesla

Anthropic’s relationship with SpaceX is also a major part of the AI company’s infrastructure plans. Its IPO filing says it expects to pay SpaceX about $3.1 billion a month once all the promised computing capacity is delivered.

"No one I know at Anthropic set off my evil detector."

Elon Musk, CEO, SpaceX and Tesla

At the Summit, Musk offered a positive assessment of Anthropic’s leadership, describing its executives as “principled” and “diligent.” Musk added that Anthropic wants additional computing capacity, potentially seeking another 10 gigawatts (GW), calling it a “big number.”

“Extremely likely that they will continue to rent compute from SpaceX.”

Elon Musk, CEO, SpaceX and Tesla

He also cautioned that demand could decline in a “worst-case scenario” if governments impose severe restrictions on AI. Musk said the agreements are short-term and either side can terminate them. He added that he would end the arrangement if he believed Anthropic was doing something “really terrible for the world.”

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TSLA stock slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past week, while chatter stayed at ‘low’ levels.

Andy Jassy: ‘We’re Big Believers In Anthropic’

Jassy reiterated Amazon’s support for Anthropic ahead of the AI company’s IPO after Anthropic disclosed details of Amazon’s ownership stake following the offering.

“We’re big believers in Anthropic.”

Andy Jassy, CEO, Amazon

Amazon is set to hold roughly 14.7% of Anthropic’s capital stock after the IPO and concurrent private placement, while Alphabet’s Google will own about 13.7%, according to the company’s filing. Together, the two companies will hold roughly 28.4%.

Jassy has previously said customers want access to multiple leading AI models, a dynamic that benefits Amazon Web Services by allowing it to offer third-party models such as Anthropic’s Claude.

At the same time, Anthropic’s filing identifies Amazon, Google and Microsoft as companies that “develop and deploy competing AI models.”

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around AMZN stock stayed in ‘bearish’ territory over the past week, accompanied by ‘low’ levels of chatter.

Microsoft, Google Have Billions Tied To Anthropic

Microsoft participated in Anthropic’s private placement, adding to its financial and commercial relationship with the AI company. Anthropic has committed to spend between $47.2 billion and $49.2 billion with Microsoft.

Alphabet’s Google is another major investor. The company agreed to purchase $10 billion in non-voting Anthropic stock through the private placement and is set to own about 13.7% of Anthropic following the transactions.

Beyond Musk and Jassy, the other Magnificent Seven CEOs did not make new public comments specifically addressing Anthropic or its IPO during the week.

That includes Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Nvidia’s Colette Kress, Apple (AAPL) CEO Tim Cook and Meta Platforms (META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ANT stock stayed in ‘extremely bullish’ territory through the week, with chatter at ‘extremely high’ levels.

data.title: Bitcoin falls to two-year low as AI valuation fears spill into crypto
data.description:
Bitcoin sank to its lowest level since September 2024 on Friday, November 20. The main spark, according to Reuters, came from outside crypto: a growing worry that investors have paid too much for artificial intelligence stocks.

That anxiety rattled markets and weighed on risk assets broadly.

Bitcoin dropped as much as 6% during the session. Intraday lows were reported between $55,533 and $57,716.

For context, that is a long way from where the asset sat a little over a year ago. Bitcoin peaked above $126,000 in October 2025 and has since lost more than 50% of its value.

The selling didn't stay politely in the spot market. Roughly $2 billion to $2.4 billion in long crypto futures positions were liquidated over a 24-hour window, and Bitcoin futures made up more than $1 billion of that total.

Institutional money was heading for the exits too. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $582 million on November 19, the day before Bitcoin reached its two-year low.

Meanwhile, the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% on November 20. When the tech-heavy index and Bitcoin take a hit on the same day for the same reason, it gets hard to argue the two live in separate worlds.

Friday's slide erased the gains Bitcoin built in the environment that followed the US election. AI valuations were the headline worry, but they weren't the only weight on the market. Concerns about the profitability of heavy AI infrastructure spending added to the gloom, along with rising borrowing costs that have dented investor confidence.

Crypto also had problems of its own making. The fallout from a Binance hack in late October still hung over the market, and Democratic gains in the midterms brought fresh regulatory uncertainty for an industry that had been counting on a friendlier policy backdrop.

Friday told a different story on Bitcoin's identity. Bitcoin traded like a high-beta tech stock, falling alongside the Nasdaq on worries that had nothing to do with blockchains, halvings or hash rates.

The ETF data deserves close attention. Spot Bitcoin ETFs were supposed to bring steady, patient institutional capital into the market. A $582 million outflow in a single day shows those same vehicles can carry money out just as efficiently as they brought it in.

Liquidations of $2 billion or more clear out a lot of overextended positions. Leverage is the other piece to watch, as thinner participation tends to mean sharper moves in both directions.

Rising borrowing costs make speculative assets less attractive compared to safer options that pay a yield, and that pressure doesn't care whether the speculative asset is an unprofitable AI startup or a cryptocurrency.

On the policy side, the midterm results add a layer of uncertainty. The industry had been operating with expectations of a more supportive Washington, and any shift in that outlook could affect everything from exchange operations to how institutions approach the sector.

The Binance hack in late October meant crypto entered this risk-off stretch already on the back foot. Bitcoin is now more than 50% below its October 2025 peak.

data.title: Chevron keeps 2027 investment decision target for $4bn Yoyo-Yolanda gas project shared by Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea
data.description:
Chevron is sticking to a 2027 target for a final investment decision on Yoyo-Yolanda, a gas field straddling the maritime border between Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, as the two governments negotiate the operating terms that must be settled before the US major can commit to spending.

The project appears with a 2027 investment decision in the table of major projects for 2025–2030 in Chevron’s investor presentation of November 5, Investir au Cameroun reported on November 20. The timetable is unchanged from the outlook Chevron presented at its investor day in November 2025, and the World Bank cited the same date in its November 4 economic report on Equatorial Guinea, the paper said.

Yoyo-Yolanda remains at the pre-front-end engineering and design (pre-FEED) stage, and none of the documents reviewed gives a date for first production, Business in Cameroon, its English-language sister publication, reported.

The fields hold an estimated 2.5 trillion cubic feet (about 70.5bn cubic metres) of gas, according to Cameroon’s Ministry of Mines. Joint studies allocate 84% of the resource to the Yoyo block on the Cameroonian side and 16% to the Yolanda block in Equatorial Guinea. Total investment has been estimated at $4bn, Business in Cameroon reported in February.

Operating agreement still under negotiation

The two countries signed a unitisation agreement on February 3 in Malabo, combining the separate Yoyo and Yolanda licences into a single unit. It built on a bilateral treaty signed in 2023, which opened the way for joint development of cross-border fields and which both parliaments had ratified and deposited with the United Nations by January 2025. The unitisation agreement sets the rules for developing the deposit jointly but does not commit anyone to building it.

The next step is a unit operating agreement with Chevron, which is still being negotiated. Delegations from Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea met in Yaoundé on November 4 to align their positions before a further round of talks with the company, Investir au Cameroun reported. In February, the two sides said discussions were continuing with the operator on the law that would apply to the production unit and on foreign-exchange rules.

Chevron holds the fields through Noble Energy Cameroon and Noble Energy EG, which it acquired with Noble Energy in 2020. Cameroon’s state hydrocarbons company, the Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures (SNH), holds a 25% stake in the Yoyo production-sharing contract, signed in 2017.

When the unitisation agreement was signed, Chevron tied the project to existing infrastructure in Equatorial Guinea. “The Yoyo-Yolanda project is central to Chevron’s strategy of supporting long-term liquefied natural gas supply and leveraging existing infrastructure at Alen and Punta Europa,” Jim Swartz, managing director for Chevron Nigeria and the mid-Africa region, said at the time, Reuters reported.

The development concept presented in February envisages a processing platform in the Yoyo area, three development wells and two export pipelines. Gas would then be processed separately at Bipaga in Cameroon and at Punta Europa on Equatorial Guinea’s Bioko Island. The concept remains a proposal that depends on further studies and the investment decision, Investir au Cameroun reported.

Gap left by Hilli

For Cameroon, the project is the main prospect for new gas output after the departure of the Hilli Episeyo floating liquefaction vessel, operated by Golar LNG , which left Kribi in August after eight years. The vessel produced about 10.8mn tonnes of LNG, loaded in 156 cargoes, from fields that SNH said had entered natural decline. SNH has identified Yoyo-Yolanda as its next major gas development, with resources far larger than the roughly 600bn cubic feet originally developed for Hilli, Business in Cameroon reported in July.

The World Bank’s 2026 economic update on Cameroon forecasts a rise in hydrocarbon exports in 2028 but does not explicitly link it to Yoyo-Yolanda, Investir au Cameroun noted.

Equatorial Guinea is further ahead with its own gas plans. Chevron took a final investment decision at the end of March on the $690mn Aseng gas project, which will tie the Aseng field back to the Alen platform and send its gas to the Punta Europa complex.

Chevron expects first gas from Aseng in 2028, Swartz said in October, Reuters reported. Malabo is counting on cross-border gas such as Yoyo-Yolanda to supply its Gas Mega Hub and keep Punta Europa running as its older fields decline.

data.title: Most new Black Democrats in decades to join US Congress, set to sway policy, party
data.description:
Key points:
  • 120th Congress brings 13 first-time Black members, largest cohort since 1993, Reuters analysis shows
  • Record seven Black senators part of new Congress after Juliana Stratton and Scott Colom victories
  • Congressional Black Caucus enters new session with record 64 members, up from 62

By Bianca Flowers, Disha Raychaudhuri and Travis Hartman

The largest class of new Black Democratic lawmakers in more than 30 years will join the US Congress in January after November's midterm elections despite Republican-led redistricting efforts, according to a Reuters analysis.

The electoral outcome sets up a test of whether increased Black representation can translate into legislative power.

Congress will include 13 new Black Democratic members, the largest cohort since 1993, House historian data showed. Four are 34 years old or younger, and more than half of Black House members were first seated in 2021 or later.

The influx of Black lawmakers could reshape Congress' legislative priorities on voting rights, healthcare affordability and economic inequality, while giving a new generation of leaders a greater voice in shaping Democratic policy, political observers say. But the lawmakers' influence will depend on whether they can translate their growing numbers into powerful committee assignments and legislative victories at a time when longstanding civil rights protections face mounting challenges.

Black candidates won 58 seats in the 435-member House for the 120th Congress, down from 61 in the current Congress, with two additional Black candidates in Louisiana headed to December 12 runoffs. Four Black Republicans will depart Congress, leaving US Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina as the only Black Republican in either chamber. Black representation in the Senate reached a record seven members following the election of Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois and the upset victory by Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom.

The shift in representation echoes the 1990s, when efforts to expand Black political representation helped usher in a new generation of lawmakers — many of whom have since gained seniority and influence, said Dedrick Asante-Muhammad, president of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies.

"This points to how important it was for a significant increase in Black representatives and how it pays off 20 to 30 years later," Asante-Muhammad said.

DIVERSE REPRESENTATION

In 1993, 16 first-time Black members joined when Congress convened, and 17 had joined by the end, the most of any Congress. Five of the current six longest-serving Black House members were first seated in 1991 or 1993.

“When you have proportional representation in Congress, it does allow for diverse representation across committees. Part of the reason why the Congressional Black Caucus formed is so that they could convince leadership to put Blacks on key committees,” said Andra Gillespie, a professor at Emory University who studies African American leadership in politics.

All current members of the caucus are Democrats.

"We're all being contacted by our constituents who are impressing upon us the need to be very bold in our approach ... to address what are crises in communities across the country," said caucus chair, US Representative Yvette Clarke, a New York Democrat, citing the affordability crisis as its members' main concern.

REDRAWN MAPS

Four districts held by Black Democrats were among those that Republican-led legislatures redrew to try to gain seats, in a push that intensified after the Supreme Court’s April ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Republicans have flipped none of the three decided so far.

Democrats Shomari Figures and Don Davis won reelection to the House in Alabama and North Carolina, respectively, while Democrat Leticia Gutierrez, who does not identify as Black, won a redrawn district in Texas previously held by Democrat Al Green.

Two Black women have a chance to secure Louisiana's remaining two congressional seats. In a majority-Black Louisiana district redrawn in May, Democrat Chauna Banks will face Republican Blake Miguez in a December 12 runoff. In a neighboring district, Democrat Patricia Moore, who led a nine-candidate field with nearly 18% of the vote, will take on Republican Gabe Firment, who received 17.2%.

US Senator Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democrat and the 11th Black senator in US history, told Reuters lawmakers must begin shaping their policy agenda before Congress convenes in January. Warnock donated to and campaigned for Colom, who will be Mississippi's first Black senator in more than 140 years.

“I’m focused on ending this war, ending these tariffs, and restoring tax credits that will bring people's healthcare costs down," Warnock said.

Most major legislation will still require bipartisan support in the Senate, and Republican President Donald Trump can veto bills passed by Congress.

NEW FACES, SENIOR LEADERS AND A TEST FOR DEMOCRATS

Black Democrats' leverage will depend on a delegation that is newer, and in some cases much younger, than in the last Congress. Melat Kiros, 29, is the first woman from Gen Z — the generation born between the late 1990s and the early 2010s — elected to Congress and the first Black woman to represent Colorado. She is one of four first-time Black House members who are 34 or younger, alongside Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adrian Boafo of Maryland, both 32, and Donavan McKinney of Michigan, 34. In contrast, the Democratic caucus’ senior Black leaders include US Representatives Maxine Waters of California, 88, and Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, 78.

“I’m unapologetically progressive. So many people are looking for bold leadership and I think that too often the messages that come out are that boldness is risky," said reelected US Representative Summer Lee, a Black Pennsylvania Democrat.

The generational mix will be tested at the top, where US Representative Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat and the favorite to become House speaker, would manage a caucus that includes moderates and progressives seeking to move the party beyond its established leadership.

“Democratic leadership is in for some trouble. (Senate Democratic leader Chuck) Schumer and Jeffries are really going to have to push back against what is going to be and has already proven to be a groundswell against their leadership,” said Periloux Peay, a political science professor at the University of Maryland.

The Congressional Black Caucus will enter the new session with a record 64 members, up from 62. Chair Clarke said she is focused on aligning progressives and moderates and expressed confidence in Jeffries.

"I'm under the impression that he's not tone deaf and that he will lead as the body requires," Clarke said.

data.title: Democrats won big in the midterms. So now what?
data.description:
Key points:
  • Democrats test whether Republicans join legislative efforts
  • Moderate-progressive fault line over universal healthcare?
  • Democrats' first 100 day agenda to be unveiled

By Richard Cowan

Democrats basking in their November 3 election wins will soon unveil an ambitious legislative agenda for the first 100 days and beyond, in a test of progressives' influence and Republicans' willingness to cooperate, as they take control of the US Congress on January 3.

That agenda is likely to be unveiled in early December once a Senate leadership race is settled.

It will mark a thunderous reversal of the past two years, when President Donald Trump's Republicans ruled the Senate and House of Representatives. With their narrow majorities, they rammed through major tax cuts skewed toward the rich and stood by as Trump grabbed their powers over tariffs and spending.

Democrats' new majorities in Congress are anything but narrow.

With a 56-44 majority in the Senate they are four votes short of the 60 votes needed to advance most legislation. In the House, their 257-172 force could grow beyond an 85-vote margin once a handful of races are settled.

"This is a realignment," said Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia in a post-election interview with reporters.

But in a warning to Democrats, veteran Republican Senator John Boozman of Arkansas said in an interview that despite his party's losses across the United States, Trump remains "a powerful force" and "I don't see any of his vetoes getting overridden" by Congress during his remaining two years in office.

AGGRESSIVE AGENDA

For months, Democrats have been plotting a House-Senate coordinated attack to undo Trump's major accomplishments, according to lawmakers and aides.

With the high cost of living the top concern voiced by voters, Democratic leaders are going after the low-hanging fruit that also would help unite their party's progressives and moderates.

Early votes are expected on legislation handcuffing Trump's ability to wage war on Iran without Congress' approval, which would help lower gasoline prices. Reversing Republicans' deep cuts to Medicaid and SNAP food stamp programs would begin helping the poor meet healthcare and grocery costs.

Meanwhile, progressives have urged raising the federal minimum wage, which is unchanged since 2009 at $7.25 per hour. Some are pushing for $20 to $25.

And in response to voter disgust over Washington ethics breaches, one of the first bills Democrats are expected to present is one barring lawmakers from insider trading of stocks.

Republicans face a bind: joining Democrats could anger Trump unless he backs measures, while stonewalling could anger voters.

"I think there's a real understanding in Congress that things like healthcare, the really exorbitant premiums, you know, that people are having to pay" must be addressed, said Boozman, who was one of the Republicans who supported around $1 trillion in cuts to Medicare, Medicaid and Obamacare programs enacted last year.

Boozman is one of the senators who would be up for re-election in 2028 and potentially open to cooperating with Democrats, although he said he would seek guidance from Trump.

'WE NEED MORE DEMOCRACY'

Newly elected progressives, who are growing in numbers in state and local offices, have a far deeper agenda for the next two years such as cutting off aid to Israel and placing a moratorium on new AI data centers.

Their to-do list also includes revamping campaign finance rules, raising taxes on the rich, writing comprehensive immigration reform and mitigating the effects of climate change.

The incoming class of members of Congress averages about eight years younger than now in the House and 14 years younger in the Senate, according to government figures.

"We'd have to actually confront monopoly power, whether it's in tech or whether it's in the utility or other major industries," said Democratic Representative-elect William Lawrence, 36, who flipped a Republican-held seat in Michigan.

"There's a lot of talk about protecting democracy. We need more democracy in the economy," Lawrence said.

Other complex issues, ranging from comprehensive immigration reform, and universal healthcare to more aggressive enforcement of environmental laws also populate an already-crowded Democratic wish list.

Retiring Democratic Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois said he has talked to colleagues about the need next year to tackle outdated laws governing work visas, the path to citizenship for migrants who lack papers and long-term border security steps, without some of the extreme deportation practices of the Trump administration.

"With the numbers that we have, we have to try to press forward, try to make a bipartisan 60 votes in the Senate" on comprehensive immigration legislation, Durbin said in a hallway interview.

IMMIGRATION, MEDICARE FOR ALL PRIORITIES

For years, many Republicans have argued Congress should hold off on sweeping immigration reforms until the southern US border is secured. Trump maintains that he has now accomplished that.

In 2013, a bipartisan immigration reform bill passed the Senate by a vote of 68-32, only to be killed by the Republican-controlled House at the time.

Meanwhile, moderate Democrats, who outnumber progressives in Congress, have largely shied away from the universal healthcare "Medicare for All" idea progressives demand. But in recent months it has been showing signs of gaining traction with more politicians and voters.

Senator Bernie Sanders has a proposal to phase in universal coverage over four years, beginning with lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 55, expanding dental, vision and hearing benefits, and guaranteeing coverage for all children.

Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine, first elected in 2008, expects to chair a House panel overseeing federal environmental spending in January.

"I think people are deeply worried about the rollback of clean air, clean water standards, climate change issues, also just the toxins in our environment," Pingree said, hinting at her 2027 subcommittee agenda.

data.title: As e-bike battery fires mount, New York weighs tougher restrictions
data.description:
By Maria Tsvetkova and Nichola Groom

They lean in apartment hallways, charge overnight in bedrooms and carry many of New York City's delivered meals. Increasingly, they are also a source of fires, linked to aging or inferior batteries.

The deaths of 10 people in two recent New York fires — at least one of them determined to be caused by e-bike batteries — prompted the New York City Council to hold an emergency hearing on Friday on a raft of stricter rules for e-bike storage and battery safety.

The three-hour meeting highlighted growing concerns among city residents about the surge in lithium-ion battery fires, which are up about 70% from a year ago. Among other measures, the proposed legislation would make it a crime to possess or use batteries that do not meet safety standards and would ban storing batteries inside apartments.

It is unclear whether the measures will advance. Officials in Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration, including from the New York City Fire Department, criticized the proposals, saying they would penalize everyday riders and low-income delivery workers.

Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the administration had "significant concerns of unintended consequences that would most heavily impact delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants, with limited English proficiency."

Delivery workers "could face losing their livelihoods and having their lives upended through the confiscation of the device they use every day to make a living," she said.

Lithium-ion battery fires have become an international concern since e-bikes and e-scooters soared in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many of those batteries are now aging, which fire officials say is likely adding to the number of fires.

Governments have taken different approaches. Britain, for instance, has focused on sellers of batteries and devices that use them.

"Unsafe e-bike and e-scooter batteries pose a serious fire risk, which is why we're strengthening the responsibility of online marketplaces and working with local authorities to remove unsafe products from sale," a British government spokesperson said in response to Reuters questions.

In the United States, the Senate unanimously passed legislation on Thursday sponsored by New York's senators, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, that would direct the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set mandatory safety standards for lithium-ion batteries used in e-bikes and other micromobility devices. The commission proposed mandatory safety standards for the batteries in June, after a public meeting in 2023. The House of Representatives has already passed the bill.

A commission staff report published in April found 45 deaths from 2017 to 2024 linked to lithium-ion battery fires involving micromobility devices: 19 tied to e-bikes, 15 to e-scooters and 11 to self-balancing scooters or hoverboards.

The issue is particularly acute in New York, where lithium-ion battery fires have reached a record this year. There were 406 such fires through early November, up from 241 in the same period last year, according to Fire Department figures cited by the City Council.

On October 28, an e-bike battery ignited in an apartment in a public housing project in the Bronx, killing four people including an 11-year-old boy. The e-bike was near the doorway, blocking the family's escape, Bonsignore said at the time.

About a week later, a fire in Sunset Park, a working-class Brooklyn neighborhood, killed six people and injured at least seven. Investigators have not determined the cause, but fire officials said two charred e-bikes were removed from the building and batteries were found in debris.

"The recent building fires in Sunset Park and in the South Bronx, which collectively claimed the lives of 10 New Yorkers, are heartbreaking tragedies that underscore the urgent need for action to prevent further loss of life,” City Council Speaker Julie Menin said at the time.

data.title: Peter Schiff Doubles Down On His ‘Black Monday’ Call Again: Ethereum Could Hit $1,000 In Two Days
data.description:
Key points:
  • Ethereum has already recovered to roughly $1,630, but it remains down more than 6% over the last 24 hours.
  • Last weekend, Peter Schiff first issued the "Black Monday" warning.
  • The Kobeissi Letter attributed the wider selloff to the Anthropic IPO, which drew cash out of markets.

Peter Schiff warned late Friday that Ethereum (ETH) could plunge to $1,000 by Monday after the token fell below the key support level of $1600.

Schiff said that there is a real risk of a crypto crash over the weekend that could send Ethereum to $1,000 by Monday. Ethereum was trading below $1,580, down over 16% since he first raised the alarm six days ago, he said. Since then, Ethereum has bounced slightly.

Ethereum’s price traded at about $1,630, down over 6% in the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around ETH improved to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’ zone, accompanied by ‘high’ chatter level over the past day.

Schiff first flagged the level on Nov. 14. He called Ethereum's chart "even more ominous" than Bitcoin's and pointed to an uptrend line near $1,600 as the line to watch. If it broke, he said the next support would be the 2022 low just under $1,000. A day later, on Nov. 15, he went further. He warned of a 'Black Monday' for Ethereum exchange-traded funds and BitMine Immersion Technologies (BMNR) if the token lost $1,600 over the weekend. Ethereum held above that level at the time.

Schiff had also predicted in April 2025 that Ethereum would reach below $1,000 but the token never fell that low.

Markets Continue To Be Under Pressure

The Kobeissi Letter, a research firm, said that the Anthropic (ANT) IPO fueled the selloff by driving cash out of the U.S. stock market. According to the firm, in the last 45 days, around $6 trillion was wiped out of the market in total, which the firm said was “sentiment is at crisis.”

Institutional investors accounted for about $400 billion of demand for the offering, while retail orders accounted for another $100 billion, the firm said. That money had to be sourced somewhere, the firm added. Kobeissi said it was drawn out just as fear was spiking, with the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), Wall Street's fear gauge, up more than 100% from its October low.

The result was a broad sell-off that simultaneously hammered stocks, gold and crypto. The research firm added that the market should stabilize once that liquidity returns.

data.title: Former Italian police chief De Gennaro takes own life amid mafia probe
data.description:
Former Italian police chief Gianni De Gennaro, who was under investigation on suspicion of obstructing a new mafia probe, has died at the age of 78, the government said on Saturday. Italian media reported that he had killed himself.

Alfredo Mantovano, undersecretary to the Prime Minister's Office, said in a statement he was "deeply shocked by the tragic death of a public servant ... whose qualities, sense of duty and commitment to the institutions I greatly admired".

De Gennaro headed the Italian police from 2000 to 2007.

One of Italy's most influential security officials over the past decades, he was found dead at his country home after relatives raised the alarm when they were unable to contact him, according to news reports.

Italy's main media outlets, including the newspapers La Repubblica and Corriere della Sera and the ANSA news agency, all said he had shot himself.

Less than a week ago, prosecutors in Caltanissetta, Sicily, named De Gennaro in an investigation into alleged efforts to obstruct inquiries into the mafia bombing in Palermo that killed anti-mafia magistrate Paolo Borsellino and five members of his escort.

Prosecutors were seeking De Gennaro's house arrest. He denied wrongdoing and no court had ruled on the allegations.

A central figure in Italy's fight against organised crime, De Gennaro had a career that stretched from the battle against the Sicilian mafia, the Cosa Nostra, to the highest levels of the police and intelligence services.

He worked closely with judge Giovanni Falcone in landmark mafia investigations during the 1980s and helped to oversee the extradition of mafia turncoat Tommaso Buscetta from Brazil.

De Gennaro later headed the Anti-Mafia Investigative Directorate (DIA), served as national police chief for seven years, and subsequently led Italy's intelligence coordination department.

His career was not without controversy. As police chief, he was at the helm of the security operation during the 2001 Group of Eight summit in Genoa, which was marred by violent clashes between police and anti-globalisation protesters.

The summit remains one of the most contentious episodes in modern Italian policing. De Gennaro consistently rejected allegations of personal wrongdoing and was ultimately acquitted in a related case.

In 2013, De Gennaro became chairman of the state-controlled aerospace and defence group Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo, a position he held until 2020.

data.title: Spain to extend banking tax to fund housing policies, PM says
data.description:
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced on Saturday his government would approve at Tuesday's cabinet meeting an extension of the current banking levy to 2027 to fund housing policies.

Sanchez last month called a snap election for November 29 in a bid to harness the momentum from massive housing protests.

  • "We will extend next the bank tax, and the revenue will go towards housing policies," Sanchez told Spanish radio station Onda Cero

  • The tax will raise €1.4 billion, Sanchez said

  • "We will allocate (the revenues) in full to the construction of social housing, tax incentives for tenants, and also the renovation of homes," Sanchez said

  • Opinion polls put the conservative People's Party (PP) ahead of Sanchez's Socialists before the election but show that it would likely need an alliance with the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox to govern

  • In December 2024, the government approved a three-year extension of the annual bank windfall tax to help citizens cope with a higher cost of living

  • The tax ranges between 1% and 7% of lenders' net interest income and commissions in accordance with their lending income volumes, instead of the previous fixed rate of 4.8%

  • For lenders whose annual volumes surpass €5 billion, it sets a rate of 7%, mainly affecting Santander , BBVA and Caixabank

data.title: Entain in talks to sell remainder of CEE business to CVC, Sky News reports
data.description:
Ladbrokes owner Entain is in advanced talks to sell its remaining stake in its central and eastern Europe operations to private equity firm CVC Capital Partners in a deal that could value the division at between £1.5 billion and £1.75 billion ($1.96 billion to $2.29 billion), Sky News reported on Saturday, citing sources.

Here are some details:

  • Entain holds a 47.5% stake in the CEE business, having offloaded a 20% interest to joint venture partner EMMA Capital in June for €425 million ($466.1 million)

  • Entain said at the time it would keep evaluating options to fully exit the business, which owns SuperSport in Croatia and STS in Poland

  • According to Sky, there are other interested parties

  • Entain is under pressure to cut costs to offset increases in Britain's gambling taxes. It expects an extra £25 million hit to its UK and Ireland retail business after the government raised taxes on the industry for a second consecutive year in last month's budget

  • Entain declined to comment on the report, while CVC did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours

data.title: The Danger of Jensen Huang's Handshake Deals at Nvidia — WSJ
data.description:
By Tim Higgins

For investors, the most worrisome thing about the entire Jensen Huang scandal isn't the sexiest stuff.

Not the mistresses. Not the suspected Chinese spying. Not the notion of his returning to Nvidia as CEO after he resigned in disgrace.

It's the suggestion that one of the most valuable, most important companies was conducting major deals between suppliers and customers on handshake agreements with Huang — and not with traditional contracts.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," Elon Musk, a major customer of Nvidia chips through his SpaceX and Tesla businesses, recently posted on X. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Such comments help explain motivations of the powerful insiders pushing for Huang's return. They aren't only showing loyalty to the man who could once make or break their companies' growth ambitions, they're trying to ensure their special connections can live on.

At stake is nothing short of the U.S. economy, which has seen a massive boost from artificial-intelligence investment with Nvidia's AI chips and Huang's dealmaking at the center. Without Huang's magic to keep it alive, some worry what will happen next. That's why those, such as Musk, President Trump and others, say Huang should get a pass on his missteps and be allowed back.

Effectively, they're arguing, Huang is bigger than the institution. He's too big to fail.

The dynamic highlights a divide in corporate governance philosophy playing out in public. A New Boys Club of pro-founders is bucking traditional safeguards and limits for the sake of growth, while others embrace more traditional corporate governance, understanding why those rules are there in the first place: continuity.

The very idea of a publicly traded company, after all, is about shared ownership, not a single irreplaceable person.

"Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing — so that is pretty magical," Satya Nadella, one of two chief executives to follow Microsoft founder Bill Gates, said this past week at the New York Times DealBook Summit. "Yes, they're singular, but they're not gods." He added, "As I used to say to Bill, founders also die so at some point a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over."

To be fair, Nvidia's remaining leadership team is arguing they can carry on without their founder. The AI chip company does rely on contracts as it competes to lock down space among third-party foundries and in-demand memory. On Tuesday, interim CEO Colette Kress tried to alleviate worries as she highlighted Nvidia's purchase commitments of $390 billion.

"It's business as usual," Kress told analysts. "We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers...They're all 100% up behind us." And she even name-checked Nvidia's most important supplier, TSMC, which makes the chips that the California company designs.

Still, Huang had long celebrated the fact that, for roughly 30 years, he did business with TSMC without formal contracts. To him, it was a sign of trust. "I don't know how many tens, hundreds of billions of dollars of business we've done through them and we don't have a contract," he told a podcaster in March. "That's pretty great."

The following month, during another podcast appearance, Huang again touted that relationship. "There's always some rough justice — sometimes I'm right, sometimes I'm wrong, sometimes I got a better deal, sometimes I got a worse deal, but overall the relationship is incredible," he said.

Supporters of Huang's approach say it played to cultural aspects of the Asian supply chain where personal relationships are currency. Or that such approaches allowed Nvidia to move fast to take advantage of a quick-moving technology. And, while Huang may have eschewed big contracts with the likes of TSMC, down in the middling ranks, there would have likely been actual purchase orders to assure quantities and prices were detailed. As microprocessor maestro Patrick Moorhead has argued, those agreements are mostly in place for at least 18 months.

"The real exposure is the next round: anything not on paper, and whether Nvidia keeps committing at Jensen's pace," the Moor Insights & Strategy founder wrote.

Part of Huang's success was the trust he developed throughout the ecosystem as something of a middleman between his technology's upstream suppliers and downstream customers. He helped build that ecosystem in part by locking up capacity with purchase agreements while using more "implicit" means — selling suppliers on a vision for the future that they believed he could deliver.

"For example, a lot of the investments that are upstream are made by our supply chain because I said to the CEOs, 'Let me tell you how big this industry is going to be, let me explain to you why, let me reason through it with you, and let me show you what I see,' " Huang said on the Dwarkesh Podcast.

If anyone should understand the downside to doing business without formal contracts, it should be Musk, who helped found OpenAI with tens of millions of dollars before things eventually turned sour.

His yearslong legal battle with OpenAI revolved around his claims that Sam Altman betrayed him by remaking the AI lab into a commercial venture. OpenAI has argued there was never any contract.

The issue around whether they had an agreement or not was never decided because a jury earlier this year rejected the lawsuit, finding the statute of limitations for bringing a case had expired. At one point during the legal battle, though, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers questioned the wisdom of Musk's pumping money into OpenAI without the terms and conditions in writing.

"It's a lot of money to do on a handshake," she said.

Musk's lawyer, who had argued emails suggested a shared understanding, replied that there was no requirement for a formal contract. "I understand there's no requirement," the federal judge said. "I'm just stating the obvious: $45 million on a handshake and what do you end up with? You end up in...court."

At the very least, you end up with uncertainty — which is what's hanging over Nvidia. Except in this instance, the proposed salve proposed through a public pressure campaign by the New Boys Club is to bring back Huang — a suggestion that, so far, the Nvidia board has rejected.

On Wednesday, Musk continued his advocacy for Huang, arguing he is irreplaceable, in part because of his personal connections. "It's like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you're on a winning streak," Musk said during a remote appearance at the Dealbook conference.

Huang may very well be the Jordan of his time, but that doesn't mean there won't be a LeBron James on the horizon.

Write to Tim Higgins at tim.higgins@wsj.com
